ingredients.intro: A one ingredient list is a short section. Here is the plant, the part of it that is usually meant, the word on the listing that we cannot reconcile, and the shell.

cards.alt: Withania somnifera with red berries in papery husks
cards.p: A small grey green shrub of dry ground, grown across India and into the Middle East and parts of Africa. It sits in the nightshade family, alongside tomato, potato and physalis, and its red berry is held in the same sort of papery husk.

The root is the part normally milled under this name, and the Sanskrit is about the root: ashva for horse, gandha for smell, after what it smells like when it is ground. Our listing does not name a part, so this page cannot state one.

cards.alt: Plain capsules and a wooden scoop on a slate board, a generated scene
cards.p: The listing calls the contents 100 per cent pure herb in one line and pure extract in another. Those are two different materials and only one can be in the jar. No extraction ratio is printed against either, and a ratio invented for a label is worse than no ratio at all.

cards.alt: Bark and root pieces at the edge of a painted nebula
cards.p: A vegan capsule, which is the one thing besides the plant that the listing names. The shell material itself is not specified, so it is not on the sheet below.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: The species is named in Latin, the serving is printed, the price is printed, and four rows on this sheet are blank, the most of any jar here, because that is the honest entry. What ashwagandha does in a person is not something we are permitted to say, so it is not on this page, and the list of reasons to ask a pharmacist first is longer here than on most jars.

reiss.label: From Reiss
reiss.h2: Powder or extract, and why the sheet says neither
paras: The listing for this jar manages to say two things at once. In one line the contents are 100 per cent pure herb. In another they are a pure extract. A milled root and an extract of a milled root are different materials, made differently, and sold at different strengths. Only one of them is in the capsule.

If it is an extract there should be a ratio, five to one or ten to one or whatever it is, and there is not one. I am not going to pick the answer that sounds better, print it, and hope. The sheet above says not resolved in that row, which is an ugly thing to have on your own product page and a true one.

This is the cheapest jar on the shelf at £17.99, and it is also the one with the most blanks. Those two facts are related and I would rather you knew both. Ring the shop and ask where the request to the supplier has got to.
